plan.topic: Black Death vs 2026: what germ theory, antibiotics and public health changed about plague
plan.angle: Plague: Black Death vs 2026, What Actually Changed. Slide 1: 'Plague in the 1300s vs today: what germ theory, antibiotics and public health changed.' Slides 2–6, 1300s vs today: cause unknown vs Yersinia pestis identified (1894); fleas and rodents not understood vs known transmission routes (CDC); no effective treatment vs antibiotics, which work best when started early (CDC/WHO); no diagnosis vs lab testing; no tracing vs contact tracing, isolation and preventive antibiotics given by health authorities. Slide 7 myths: 'extinct': still occurs naturally, with an average of 7 human cases a year in the US (CDC, range 0–17). 'Untreatable': treatable with antibiotics, and prompt treatment is critical (CDC). Slide 8: red flags after possible exposure, plus 'contact a doctor or local health authority urgently'. Label death tolls as estimates, no doom words or graphic imagery, and close with 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
plan.working_title: Plague: Black Death vs 2026, What Actually Changed
plan.why: This is our evergreen and myth slot. It's a comparison that names both sides, has long-tail search value (RTE and Slate are revisiting the history), hasn't been covered yet, and works as a list people save. | fact-check: A good history-vs-now framework, and the facts check out: Yersin identified the bacterium in 1894, and CDC reports an average of 7 human cases a year (range 0–17). Problem: slide 1's hook 'Could the Black Death happen again?' is the doom framing the guardrails ban. Rewrite it as a calm comparison. In the 'no treatment' cell, say 'no effective treatment (antibiotics didn't exist)'. Label death tolls as estimates (e.g. 'estimated 30–50% of Europe's population'). On slide 7, write 'treatable, especially when antibiotics start early'. 'Contact tracing … and preventive antibiotics given by health authorities' must keep the authority wording.

package.title: Plague: Black Death vs 2026, What Actually Changed

social.instagram_caption:
Same germ, very different playbook: the 1300s vs 2026.

In the 1300s, nobody knew what caused plague.
In 1894, Alexandre Yersin (and, independently, Kitasato Shibasaburo) identified the bacterium now called Yersinia pestis (Britannica).
Today, lab tests confirm plague (WHO), and antibiotics can cure it if treatment starts early (WHO, CDC).
Pneumonic plague is the only form that can spread between people, and CDC says person-to-person spread hasn't been documented in the US since 1924.

After a possible exposure (flea bites or sick animals in plague areas, or close contact with a pneumonic patient), contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Red flags (CDC): fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, swollen painful lymph nodes.

Save this for your next history deep-dive or plague-in-the-news moment.

What surprises you more: that no one knew the cause back then, or that CDC counts an average of 5 human plague cases a year in the US in recent decades (range 0–17)?

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

factcheck.summary:
The carousel is accurate and safe, and it delivers what the title promises. I checked every claim against the live sources:
- **US cases:** CDC currently says "an average of five human plague cases are reported each year" (range 0–17), mostly in northern New Mexico and Arizona. The page was last reviewed on 7 Oct 2026. The 5-a-year figure on slide 6 is correct. The older "7 a year" figure in the playbook is out of date.
- **How plague spreads:** the CDC page says droplets are "the only way that plague can spread between people", and that there has been no US person-to-person spread since 1924.
- **WHO fact sheet (updated 29 Sep 2026):**
  - Common antibiotics can cure plague when given early.
  - Lab confirmation of Y. pestis.
  - Most cases in 2019–2025 were in DR Congo and Madagascar.
  - Close contacts are traced and given 7 days of preventive antibiotics.
  - Pneumonic patients are isolated.
- **Symptoms:** they match CDC's list.
- **Curability:** CDC's "can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly" is quoted correctly.
- **1894:** Britannica's text ("In 1894 Yersin was sent to Hong Kong, where he and Kitasato Shibasaburo independently discovered the plague bacillus") was confirmed through search. The page itself blocks automated fetching (403).

Safety is fine. The red flags are tied to possible exposure and say to contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Slide 5 warns against self-treatment and stockpiling, and the CTA carries the "If you're worried, talk to a health professional." line. There is no fear-bait. The 1300s column is honestly labelled as general historical context.

There are only minor fixes: one wording addition on slide 6, one unsourced "same germ" claim, and one source metadata date.

issues.claim: CDC: an average of 5 human cases a year in recent decades (range 0–17)
issues.problem: The CDC page says 'An average of five human plague cases are reported each year' (range 0–17). The words 'in recent decades' don't appear on the page. They're a small addition we made and attributed to CDC.
issues.fix: CDC: an average of 5 human plague cases are reported each year in the US (range 0–17), mostly in the western US, especially northern New Mexico and Arizona. WHO: most cases reported in 2019–2025 were in DR Congo and Madagascar.

issues.claim: Same germ. Very different playbook. / Same germ, better tools
issues.problem: None of the listed sources supports the claim that the Black Death was caused by Y. pestis. It's well established through ancient DNA (Bos et al., Nature 2011), but it has no source here.
issues.fix: Add this source: {"id":"bos-2011-nature","title":"A draft genome of Yersinia pestis from victims of the Black Death","publisher":"Nature (Bos KI et al.)","year":"2011","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3690193"}. Then append to the slide 2 body: "Ancient DNA from 1348–1350 London victims confirms the Black Death was Y. pestis (Bos et al., Nature 2011)."

issues.problem: The live page shows 'Updated: August 24, 2026', so the year is wrong.
issues.fix: Set the title to "About Plague (updated 24 Aug 2026)" and the year to "2026".
